scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
Remember the bigger engagement I mentioned on your first day? It's here.

**Neo Smart Living** — the Southern California company behind the Tahoe Mini backyard unit — has issued a formal RFP, and it could become the largest engagement of our year. They're not asking for a single study. They need to decide how to **position**, **feature**, and **price** a $23,000 product, and their objectives span everything from market landscape to idea generation to hard measurement.

That means you're not choosing a method this time. You're designing a **research program**: exactly **three** components that work together, inside a budget of **$60,000** and a **14-week** window.

Work backward from their decision. Ask what each component contributes that the others can't, watch for options that duplicate each other, and add up the invoice before you submit. The full RFP is in your **Inbox**, along with a note from Marcus on building multi-method programs. I'll be reviewing this one personally.

— Dana

inbox.subject: Neo Smart Living RFP — the big one
inbox.body:
The Neo Smart Living RFP is attached. Read it more than once.

Three things to notice as you read. First, their objectives come in **three distinct families** — facts about the market, ideas and language from homeowners, and numbers that project to their target market. A proposal that nails one family and ignores the others will lose to a competitor's program. Second, the **constraints are real**: $60,000 total, findings in 14 weeks. Every component you propose draws from the same pot. Third, they sell a product most people have never considered buying — so *how homeowners talk about backyard space* matters as much as *how many* would pay $23,000 for it.

Select the three components that, together, cover all three families of objectives without duplicating each other or busting the budget. This proposal carries my signature and yours.

— Dana

attachments.title: Request for Proposal — Neo Smart Living
attachments.body:
**Neo Smart Living — Request for Proposal**

**Company background.** Neo Smart Living is a Southern California company that designs and installs compact, factory-built backyard units. Our flagship product, the **Tahoe Mini**, is a 117-square-foot unit (9 ft × 13 ft) advertised from $19,800 and priced at **$23,000 delivered and installed**, inclusive of tax and warranty. The Tahoe Mini is *not* an accessory dwelling unit: it has no plumbing or kitchen and is classified as a non-habitable accessory structure. It is intentionally sized under California's roughly 120-square-foot permit threshold, so most installations require no building permit (homeowner-association and local rules still apply). Units ship as flat-packed modular panels and install in most backyards in a single day. Standard equipment includes pre-wired electrical, a smart entry lock, dual-pane floor-to-ceiling glass, and a pitched roof with drainage. Optional upgrades include sound insulation, mini-split heating and cooling, and privacy panel swaps. Our catalog also includes the **Mojave**, an expandable container tiny home (up to 400 square feet expanded, full kitchen and bathroom, $35,800): it serves a different market and is **out of scope for this engagement**, which concerns the Tahoe Mini line only.

**Business decision.** Over the next two quarters, leadership must decide how to **position** the Tahoe Mini line, which **features** to make standard versus optional, and whether the **$23,000 price** should hold, rise, or fall. These are linked decisions, and we intend to make them on evidence.

**Target market.** Owner-occupied single-family homeowners in Southern California with usable yard space, ages 30–65, household income $75,000 or more, interested in flexible space for remote work, wellness, or hosting guests.

**Research objectives.** We seek a partner to propose an integrated program addressing three families of questions:

- **Market landscape.** What is the size, growth, and competitive structure of the prefab backyard-structure category? Who are the competitors, at what prices, and what trends are documented? We expect much of this is already published.
- **Ideas and reactions.** How do homeowners in our target market talk about backyard space? What uses, features, and concerns come up spontaneously? How do they react to positioning concepts and to the unit itself? We want depth and language here, not statistics.
- **Measurement.** Among our target market, what proportion finds the concept appealing? Which features add the most value? What do homeowners expect a unit like this to cost? Results must be projectable to the target market described above.

**Constraints.** Total research budget: **$60,000**. Findings required within **14 weeks**. We expect the selected partner to propose a program of complementary components rather than a single study, and to sequence them sensibly.

**Contact.** E. Navarro, Chief Executive Officer, Neo Smart Living.

inbox.subject: Advice: proposing a program, not a method
inbox.body:
Heard you drew the Neo proposal — congratulations and condolences. Three things I do on every multi-method RFP:

1. **Sequence cheap-to-expensive.** Secondary research first (it's fast and cheap, and it tells the later studies what to ask), qualitative second (it generates the ideas and language), quantitative last (it measures what the first two surfaced). Landscape → ideas → numbers.
2. **One component per objective family.** If two options answer the same family of questions, the second one is usually a trap — you're paying twice for coverage you already bought.
3. **Do the arithmetic.** Add up your three investments *before* you fall in love with them. Then check geography and scope: a study of the wrong population is worse than no study, because it looks like evidence.

Dana's watching this one, so make the reasoning airtight. You've got this.

— Marcus

pages.title: Neo Smart Living — Research Program Selection
pages.intro: Based on Neo Smart Living's RFP (see the Inbox), select the **three** components of your proposed research program. Together they must cover Neo's landscape, ideation, and measurement objectives — within **$60,000** and **14 weeks**. Review every row, and total your investments before submitting.

tasks.title: Neo Smart Living Research Program
tasks.prompt: Select the **three** components that best cover Neo's objectives — market landscape, ideas and reactions, and projectable measurement — within budget and timeline.

cells.name: Secondary Research
cells.desc: Review of 10–15 industry and housing sources: prefab backyard-structure market size, competitor landscape and pricing, category trends, and permit-threshold context
cells.deliverable: Landscape report with competitive price map
cells.geo: North America category | SoCal housing context

cells.name: Focus Groups
cells.desc: Four groups of 8 Southern California homeowners from the target market, exploring backyard-space language, spontaneous uses and concerns, and reactions to positioning concepts and the Tahoe Mini

cells.name: Survey
cells.desc: Online survey of Southern California owner-occupied single-family homeowners measuring concept appeal, feature value, and price expectations

cells.name: Extended Secondary Research
cells.desc: Exhaustive review of 30+ industry, housing, and economic sources covering the category landscape in maximum depth
cells.geo: North America category | SoCal housing context

cells.name: National Survey
cells.desc: Large-scale online survey of U.S. homeowners nationwide on backyard-structure appeal and price expectations

cells.name: In-depth Interviews — City Officials
cells.desc: 10 one-on-one interviews with Southern California city planning officials on accessory-structure rules, enforcement, and likely regulatory direction

cells.name: Mystery Shopping
cells.desc: Trained shoppers visit competitor showrooms and dealer lots, logging sales pitches, pricing offers, and service standards
cells.deliverable: Individual report per interaction | Summary report

cells.name: Experiment — Two-Price Market Test
cells.desc: In-market A/B test offering the Tahoe Mini at two price points in matched territories; compare inquiry and order rates

cells.name: Observational Research
cells.desc: Unobtrusive observation of shoppers in the outdoor-structure aisles of home-improvement retailers (subjects in public retail spaces)

guides.title: Round 3 — Choosing a Research Program, Not Just a Method
guides.body:
**When one method isn't enough.** Big decisions — positioning, features, and pricing together — usually need evidence of more than one kind. The classic mixed-methods sequence:

| Phase | Method family | What it contributes |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Landscape | Secondary research | Fast, cheap facts that already exist: market size, competitors, prices, trends. Also sharpens the questions for later phases |
| 2. Explore | Qualitative (focus groups, interviews) | Ideas, language, spontaneous reactions — what to measure, and the words to measure it in |
| 3. Measure | Quantitative (survey, experiment) | Projectable numbers: how many, how much, which features, what price |

**Secondary → qualitative → quantitative.** Each phase feeds the next: the landscape tells the groups what to probe; the groups tell the survey what to ask.

**Rules for assembling the program:**

- **Cover every objective family once.** Map each RFP objective to exactly one component. A program that measures twice but never explores is unbalanced — and so is the reverse.
- **Don't pay for the same coverage twice.** Two options that answer the same questions differ only in cost. The bigger one is rarely worth it.
- **Do the budget arithmetic.** Total your components' investments and compare against the client's ceiling *before* submitting. Timeline too: phases can overlap somewhat, but a single component that nearly fills the whole window leaves no room for the rest.
- **Match the geography to the decision.** Data about people who can't buy the product is not evidence, no matter how large the sample.
